title: Weak square-integrable derivatives give integrable Fourier moments
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field] and Lebesgue measure on $\mathbf R^m$, where $m\geq1$. Write $L^2(\mathbf R^m;\mathbf C)$ for measurable square-integrable complex functions modulo almost-everywhere equality. For $u$ in this space, let $\widehat u$ be its Plancherel Fourier transform: the continuous extension to $L^2$ of $f\mapsto(\xi\mapsto\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx)$ on Schwartz functions (smooth functions all of whose derivatives decrease faster than every inverse polynomial). Let $t,r\geq0$ be integers with $t>r+m/2$. Assume that for every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbf N^m$ with $|\alpha|\leq t$ there is $u_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbf R^m;\mathbf C)$ satisfying $\int u_\alpha\phi=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int u\,\partial^\alpha\phi$ for every compactly supported smooth complex test function $\phi$; here $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$ and $\partial^\alpha=\prod_i\partial_{x_i}^{\alpha_i}$. Then, for every integer $0\leq j\leq r$, $$\int_{\mathbf R^m}\|\xi\|^j|\widehat u(\xi)|\,d\xi<\infty.$$ The assertion is independent of the measurable representative of $\widehat u$.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2, Sobolev lemma (2.1), printed p.289. The Euclidean weighted-Fourier integrability input for (2.1), before inverse transformation. proof.text: Choose a measurable representative $h$ of $\widehat u$; by the definition of the Plancherel transform, $h\in L^2$. For each coordinate $i$, apply [lem-sfb-l2-weak-derivative-fourier-identity] to $u$, $u_{t e_i}$ and the multi-index $t e_i$. Its weak-derivative hypothesis is exactly the assumed test identity, since $|t e_i|=t$. Its conclusion gives $\xi_i^t h\in L^2$ for every $i$.

proof.text: Put $w(\xi)=1+\|\xi\|^2$ and $M(\xi)=\max(1,|\xi_1|^2,\ldots,|\xi_m|^2)$. Then $w\leq(m+1)M$ and $M^t\leq1+\sum_i|\xi_i|^{2t}$. Thus $$w^t|h|^2\leq(m+1)^t\bigl(|h|^2+\sum_i|\xi_i^t h|^2\bigr).$$ The right side has finite integral by step 1 and finite additivity of the integral; integrating this nonnegative inequality shows that the measurable function $a=w^{t/2}|h|$ is square-integrable. This is elementary finite-sum arithmetic and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral; no comparison of Sobolev definitions is used.

proof.text: Fix an integer $0\leq j\leq r$. Then $s=t-j>m/2$, so [lem-sfb-euclidean-bracket-integrable] gives $\int w^{j-t}<\infty$. Define the measurable nonnegative function $b=\|\xi\|^j w^{-t/2}$. Since $\|\xi\|^{2j}\leq w^j$, one has $b^2\leq w^{j-t}$, and integration proves $b\in L^2$. All real powers have positive base $w\geq1$; when $j=0$ the numerator is the constant $1$, including at $\xi=0$.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2 (2.1), printed p.289. Agent-written Euclidean Fourier argument supporting Sobolev embedding; Mathlib/Analysis/Distribution/Sobolev.lean:241–275 supplies the related weighted L2 product calculation, not the weak-derivative bridge.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-l2-product-integrable] to the real-valued functions $a,b$ of steps 2 and 3, whose measurability and square integrability have been established. Their product is exactly $ab=\|\xi\|^j|h(\xi)|$, because $w^{t/2}w^{-t/2}=1$. Hence the required Fourier moment has finite integral for each $0\leq j\leq r$.

proof.text: If $h'$ is another measurable representative, then $h'=h$ off a null set. Multiplication by the everywhere finite weight $\|\xi\|^j$ preserves this almost-everywhere equality of absolute values. Their nonnegative integrals are therefore equal, proving independence of the representative.
